SECTION 2: PROJECT BACKGROUND

The Lagos Port Complex (LPC) is the principal gateway for Nigeria’s international trade, handling in excess of 60% of the country’s seaborne cargo throughput. Berths 9 and 10 are dedicated general cargo and container berths located on the eastern arm of the port’s main quay wall. The original berth design from the 1970s provided for a maintained depth of 11.5 metres below chart datum (CD). Over the years, repeated maintenance dredging has been carried out to retain this depth, but the port has experienced periodic siltation problems, particularly along the inner section of the approach channel adjacent to the berth pockets.

The current contract was awarded in November 2020 following an open tendering process. The scope of works includes capital dredging of the berth pocket and approach channel to a depth of 13.0 metres below CD, placement of rock armour along the toe of the existing quay wall where scour has been noted, and disposal of dredged material at the designated offshore disposal site approximately 18 nautical miles south-west of the port entrance. A pre-dredge bathymetric survey was completed in January 2021 by the contractor’s survey team using a multi-beam echo sounder, and the results were submitted under cover letter WATS/LPC/2021/0042.

Since the award of the contract, the following developments have occurred:

- The Nigerian Ports Authority issued its Revised Vessel Access and Channel Management Policy in January 2021, which recommends a minimum maintained depth of 14.5 metres below CD for berths handling vessels with a draught of up to 13.5 metres.
- The LPA has received firm commitments from two major shipping lines to introduce a new class of container vessels (approximately 8,500 TEU) on the Europe–West Africa route, with an expected first call at Lagos in the fourth quarter of 2021. These vessels have a design draught of 13.8 metres.
- A geotechnical investigation report (Ref. GEO/WATS/2021/011) completed in February 2021 identified a thin layer of stiff clay and dense sand at depths between 13.0 and 15.5 metres below CD across the berth pocket. The report confirms that these materials are readily dredgeable with the contractor’s existing trailing suction hopper dredger, CSD-3 "Ogun".

It is in this context that the contractor proposes to increase the dredging depth to better future-proof the port’s capacity and to avoid the need for a further capital dredging campaign within the next 5–7 years.

SECTION 3: JUSTIFICATION

The justification for this change request is based on three principal considerations: (i) compliance with updated regulatory guidance, (ii) alignment with the client’s stated future vessel traffic ambitions, and (iii) technical feasibility and cost efficiency.

3.1 Regulatory Compliance

NPA’s January 2021 policy document sets out recommended depth parameters for various berth categories. For berths in the general cargo/container category within the Lagos Port Complex, the policy recommends a maintained depth of at least 14.5 metres below CD. The current contract specification of 13.0 metres below CD falls short of this recommendation. By increasing the dredging depth to 15.0 metres, the port will not only meet the current recommendation but also provide an additional safety margin of 0.5 metres to account for siltation between dredging campaigns.

SECTION 5: SCHEDULE IMPACT

The contractor has reviewed the programme of works and confirms that the additional dredging volume can be accommodated within the existing contract duration without the need for an extension of time, subject to the following conditions:

- Approval of this change request is granted on or before 31 March 2021.
- The deepening works are executed concurrently with the already-planned dredging activities in the berth pocket and approach channel.
- The contractor’s trailing suction hopper dredger CSD-3 "Ogun" remains available without unplanned breakdown or dry-docking requirements.

The additional volume of 185,000 m³ will require approximately 24 additional working days of dredging, based on the production rates achieved during the first two months of the contract. This additional time will be absorbed by re-sequencing the dredging activities, prioritising the deeper areas first, and utilising the standby periods that are already built into the programme for weather and tide delays.

No change to the contract completion date is proposed. The contractor will issue a revised dredging sequence plan within 14 days of approval of this change request for the Engineer’s review and acceptance.

Source format: Engineering review memo

This memo documents the engineering review of Change Request CR-2021-07, submitted on 28 April 2021 by the Port Operations Department. The request seeks approval to revise the contractual dredging depth for the Berth 4 approach channel from the originally specified -14.5 m CD to -15.2 m CD. The purpose of this review is to assess the technical feasibility of the proposed change, evaluate potential impacts on dredging works already executed, and provide a recommendation to the Contracting Office for the formal variation process.

2. BACKGROUND

2.1 Original Contract Scope
The dredging contract for the Berth 4 approach channel, Contract No. LPA/CON/DRG/2020/118, was awarded in August 2020 to Messrs. Niger Delta Dredging Consortium (NDDC). The original scope required dredging of the approach channel to a design depth of -14.5 m CD over a width of 180 m and a length of approximately 2.4 km, measured from the channel entrance buoy to the berthing pocket at Berth 4. The contract stipulated a total dredged volume of approximately 1,850,000 m³, with a completion period of 18 months from the date of possession of the site.

2.2 Background to the Change Request
Port Operations Department has observed, over the past two dry seasons, that vessels with drafts of up to 13.8 m have experienced occasional under-keel clearance (UKC) values below the minimum 1.0 m required by the port's safety policy. This has occurred during spring tides when the tidal window is limited, and at certain states of the tide when the actual water level falls short of predicted chart datum levels. The Operations Department therefore proposed, and the Harbour Master's Office concurred, that the approach channel depth be increased to -15.2 m CD to provide a more robust UKC margin for the larger vessels now regularly calling at Berth 4.

2.3 Requested Change
CR-2021-07 proposes the following variation to the contract:
- Increase the dredging depth from -14.5 m CD to -15.2 m CD over the full length and width of the approach channel as originally defined.
- The additional dredging volume is estimated at approximately 310,000 m³, based on the initial survey data submitted by NDDC.
- The contract completion period to be extended by 8 weeks to account for the additional dredging works.
- The contract price to be adjusted by the additional quantities at the applicable bill rates, plus provisional allowances for any rock encountered below the current design depth.

Change Request CR-2021-07 status pending_approval. Record status: current.

3. TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY ANALYSIS

3.1 Sub-surface Conditions
Review of the pre-contract geotechnical investigation report (Ref: LPA/ENG/GEO/2020/045, Boreholes BH-01 to BH-12) indicates that the sub-surface profile along the Berth 4 approach channel consists primarily of the following layers, in descending order:
- Soft to firm silty clay, generally encountered from the existing bed level to approximately -12.0 m CD.
- Medium dense to dense silty sand, encountered from approximately -12.0 m CD to -20.0 m CD.
- Stiff to hard clay, encountered below -20.0 m CD at most borehole locations.

The proposed deepening to -15.2 m CD would therefore require dredging within the medium dense to dense silty sand layer. This material is generally suitable for dredging using a trailing suction hopper dredger (TSHD) or a cutter suction dredger (CSD). The grain size distribution from the laboratory tests indicates a mean particle size (D50) ranging from 0.18 mm to 0.35 mm, which is well within the capability of both dredger types.

3.2 Dredging Equipment Suitability
NDDC's current dredging fleet, as mobilised for this contract, comprises:
- TSHD "Niger Delta Queen" (6,500 m³ hopper capacity, with a maximum dredging depth of -25 m CD)
- CSD "Port Harcourt Pride" (with a maximum dredging depth of -18 m CD)
- Two (2) split hopper barges (1,200 m³ each)
- One (1) survey launch and associated echo-sounding equipment
The proposed deepening to -15.2 m CD will require removal of material from the medium dense to dense silty sand layer. Based on the grain size distribution and the layer thickness, the following is the engineering assessment of the proposed methodology:

Production rate estimates, based on the original contract data and adjusted for the medium dense sand, are as follows:

- TSHD: 4,500 m³ per operational day (based on a 20-hour working day, including transit time to the disposal ground).
- CSD: 3,200 m³ per operational day (based on a 20-hour working day, including pipeline and barge turnaround).

The total additional volume of approximately 310,000 m³ is therefore estimated to require about 70 to 80 operational days of dredging, which is consistent with the proposed 8-week extension of time, allowing for weather downtime and mobilisation.

3.4 Environmental and Navigational Considerations

The deepening of the approach channel will result in a temporary increase in turbidity within the dredging area and along the disposal route. The following conditions are recommended to mitigate environmental impacts:

- Continuous monitoring of suspended solids at three (3) fixed stations, located at the dredging face, the mid-channel, and the entrance to the port basin.
- Suspension of dredging operations if the suspended solids concentration at the mid-channel station exceeds 150 mg/l above background levels for a continuous period of more than 2 hours.
- Use of a silt curtain around the CSD operations when working within 200 m of the Berth 4 quay wall.

From a navigational perspective, the deepening will improve the under-keel clearance for vessels transiting the channel. However, during the dredging period, the presence of the TSHD and the CSD will restrict the available width of the channel. A temporary traffic management plan will be required, to be agreed with the Port Harbour Master's office prior to commencement.

4.0 REVIEW OF SUPPORTING DATA AND SURVEYS

4.1 Hydrographic Survey Adequacy

The pre-contract survey (Ref: LPA/HYD/2020/118) and the recent survey (Ref: LPA/HYD/2021/031) have been reviewed. The recent survey coverage is considered adequate for the main channel area. However, the survey density in the berth pocket itself is lower than the standard specified in the contract (i.e., 10 m line spacing). It is therefore a condition of approval that a supplementary pre-dredging survey of the berth pocket and the immediate turning area be carried out to confirm the actual bed levels in this zone.

4.2 Geotechnical Data

The geotechnical investigation report (Ref: LPA/ENG/GEO/2020/045) is based on boreholes BH-01 to BH-12. The borehole spacing along the channel is considered sufficient for the general assessment of the sub-surface profile. However, it is noted that the report does not include any borehole in the immediate vicinity of the berth pocket. Given the presence of stiff to hard clay below -20.0 m CD, and the possibility of isolated pockets of cemented sand or laterite in the medium dense sand layer, it is recommended that the dredging contractor be required to:

- Carry out trial pits or probe soundings at a minimum of three (3) locations within the berth pocket area prior to commencement of the deepening works.
- Report any material encountered that is not consistent with the geotechnical profile described in the report, for a potential re-classification of the material and a review of the applicable bill rates.

SECTION 2: PROJECT BACKGROUND

The Lagos Port Complex (LPC) is the principal gateway for Nigeria’s international trade, handling in excess of 60% of the country’s seaborne cargo throughput. Berths 9 and 10 are dedicated general cargo and container berths located on the eastern arm of the port’s main quay wall. The original berth design from the 1970s provided for a maintained depth of 11.5 metres below chart datum (CD). Over the years, repeated maintenance dredging has been carried out to retain this depth, but the port has experienced periodic siltation problems, particularly along the inner section of the approach channel adjacent to the berth pockets.

The current contract was awarded in November 2020 following an open tendering process. The scope of works includes capital dredging of the berth pocket and approach channel to a depth of 13.0 metres below CD, placement of rock armour along the toe of the existing quay wall where scour has been noted, and disposal of dredged material at the designated offshore disposal site approximately 18 nautical miles south-west of the port entrance. A pre-dredge bathymetric survey was completed in January 2021 by the contractor’s survey team using a multi-beam echo sounder, and the results were submitted under cover letter WATS/LPC/2021/0042.

Since the award of the contract, the following developments have occurred:

- The Nigerian Ports Authority issued its Revised Vessel Access and Channel Management Policy in January 2021, which recommends a minimum maintained depth of 14.5 metres below CD for berths handling vessels with a draught of up to 13.5 metres.
- The LPA has received firm commitments from two major shipping lines to introduce a new class of container vessels (approximately 8,500 TEU) on the Europe–West Africa route, with an expected first call at Lagos in the fourth quarter of 2021. These vessels have a design draught of 13.8 metres.
- A geotechnical investigation report (Ref. GEO/WATS/2021/011) completed in February 2021 identified a thin layer of stiff clay and dense sand at depths between 13.0 and 15.5 metres below CD across the berth pocket. The report confirms that these materials are readily dredgeable with the contractor’s existing trailing suction hopper dredger, CSD-3 "Ogun".

It is in this context that the contractor proposes to increase the dredging depth to better future-proof the port’s capacity and to avoid the need for a further capital dredging campaign within the next 5–7 years.

The justification for this change request is based on three principal considerations: (i) compliance with updated regulatory guidance, (ii) alignment with the client’s stated future vessel traffic ambitions, and (iii) technical feasibility and cost efficiency.

NPA’s January 2021 policy document sets out recommended depth parameters for various berth categories. For berths in the general cargo/container category within the Lagos Port Complex, the policy recommends a maintained depth of at least 14.5 metres below CD. The current contract specification of 13.0 metres below CD falls short of this recommendation. By increasing the dredging depth to 15.0 metres, the port will not only meet the current recommendation but also provide an additional safety margin of 0.5 metres to account for siltation between dredging campaigns.

documents.title: Engineering Review Memo – CR-2021-07
documents.content:
This memo documents the engineering review of Change Request CR-2021-07, submitted on 28 April 2021 by the Port Operations Department. The request seeks approval to revise the contractual dredging depth for the Berth 4 approach channel from the originally specified -14.5 m CD to -15.2 m CD. The purpose of this review is to assess the technical feasibility of the proposed change, evaluate potential impacts on dredging works already executed, and provide a recommendation to the Contracting Office for the formal variation process.

2. BACKGROUND

2.1 Original Contract Scope
The dredging contract for the Berth 4 approach channel, Contract No. LPA/CON/DRG/2020/118, was awarded in August 2020 to Messrs. Niger Delta Dredging Consortium (NDDC). The original scope required dredging of the approach channel to a design depth of -14.5 m CD over a width of 180 m and a length of approximately 2.4 km, measured from the channel entrance buoy to the berthing pocket at Berth 4. The contract stipulated a total dredged volume of approximately 1,850,000 m³, with a completion period of 18 months from the date of possession of the site.

2.2 Background to the Change Request
Port Operations Department has observed, over the past two dry seasons, that vessels with drafts of up to 13.8 m have experienced occasional under-keel clearance (UKC) values below the minimum 1.0 m required by the port's safety policy. This has occurred during spring tides when the tidal window is limited, and at certain states of the tide when the actual water level falls short of predicted chart datum levels. The Operations Department therefore proposed, and the Harbour Master's Office concurred, that the approach channel depth be increased to -15.2 m CD to provide a more robust UKC margin for the larger vessels now regularly calling at Berth 4.

2.3 Requested Change
CR-2021-07 proposes the following variation to the contract:
- Increase the dredging depth from -14.5 m CD to -15.2 m CD over the full length and width of the approach channel as originally defined.
- The additional dredging volume is estimated at approximately 310,000 m³, based on the initial survey data submitted by NDDC.
- The contract completion period to be extended by 8 weeks to account for the additional dredging works.
- The contract price to be adjusted by the additional quantities at the applicable bill rates, plus provisional allowances for any rock encountered below the current design depth.

Change Request CR-2021-07 status pending_approval. Record status: current.

3. TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY ANALYSIS

3.1 Sub-surface Conditions
Review of the pre-contract geotechnical investigation report (Ref: LPA/ENG/GEO/2020/045, Boreholes BH-01 to BH-12) indicates that the sub-surface profile along the Berth 4 approach channel consists primarily of the following layers, in descending order:
- Soft to firm silty clay, generally encountered from the existing bed level to approximately -12.0 m CD.
- Medium dense to dense silty sand, encountered from approximately -12.0 m CD to -20.0 m CD.
- Stiff to hard clay, encountered below -20.0 m CD at most borehole locations.

The proposed deepening to -15.2 m CD would therefore require dredging within the medium dense to dense silty sand layer. This material is generally suitable for dredging using a trailing suction hopper dredger (TSHD) or a cutter suction dredger (CSD). The grain size distribution from the laboratory tests indicates a mean particle size (D50) ranging from 0.18 mm to 0.35 mm, which is well within the capability of both dredger types.

3.2 Dredging Equipment Suitability
NDDC's current dredging fleet, as mobilised for this contract, comprises:
- TSHD "Niger Delta Queen" (6,500 m³ hopper capacity, with a maximum dredging depth of -25 m CD)
- CSD "Port Harcourt Pride" (with a maximum dredging depth of -18 m CD)
- Two (2) split hopper barges (1,200 m³ each)
- One (1) survey launch and associated echo-sounding equipment

documents.title: Engineering Review Memo – CR-2021-07
documents.content:
The proposed deepening to -15.2 m CD will require removal of material from the medium dense to dense silty sand layer. Based on the grain size distribution and the layer thickness, the following is the engineering assessment of the proposed methodology:

Production rate estimates, based on the original contract data and adjusted for the medium dense sand, are as follows:

- TSHD: 4,500 m³ per operational day (based on a 20-hour working day, including transit time to the disposal ground).
- CSD: 3,200 m³ per operational day (based on a 20-hour working day, including pipeline and barge turnaround).

The total additional volume of approximately 310,000 m³ is therefore estimated to require about 70 to 80 operational days of dredging, which is consistent with the proposed 8-week extension of time, allowing for weather downtime and mobilisation.

3.4 Environmental and Navigational Considerations

The deepening of the approach channel will result in a temporary increase in turbidity within the dredging area and along the disposal route. The following conditions are recommended to mitigate environmental impacts:

- Continuous monitoring of suspended solids at three (3) fixed stations, located at the dredging face, the mid-channel, and the entrance to the port basin.
- Suspension of dredging operations if the suspended solids concentration at the mid-channel station exceeds 150 mg/l above background levels for a continuous period of more than 2 hours.
- Use of a silt curtain around the CSD operations when working within 200 m of the Berth 4 quay wall.

From a navigational perspective, the deepening will improve the under-keel clearance for vessels transiting the channel. However, during the dredging period, the presence of the TSHD and the CSD will restrict the available width of the channel. A temporary traffic management plan will be required, to be agreed with the Port Harbour Master's office prior to commencement.

4.0 REVIEW OF SUPPORTING DATA AND SURVEYS

4.1 Hydrographic Survey Adequacy

The pre-contract survey (Ref: LPA/HYD/2020/118) and the recent survey (Ref: LPA/HYD/2021/031) have been reviewed. The recent survey coverage is considered adequate for the main channel area. However, the survey density in the berth pocket itself is lower than the standard specified in the contract (i.e., 10 m line spacing). It is therefore a condition of approval that a supplementary pre-dredging survey of the berth pocket and the immediate turning area be carried out to confirm the actual bed levels in this zone.

4.2 Geotechnical Data

The geotechnical investigation report (Ref: LPA/ENG/GEO/2020/045) is based on boreholes BH-01 to BH-12. The borehole spacing along the channel is considered sufficient for the general assessment of the sub-surface profile. However, it is noted that the report does not include any borehole in the immediate vicinity of the berth pocket. Given the presence of stiff to hard clay below -20.0 m CD, and the possibility of isolated pockets of cemented sand or laterite in the medium dense sand layer, it is recommended that the dredging contractor be required to:

- Carry out trial pits or probe soundings at a minimum of three (3) locations within the berth pocket area prior to commencement of the deepening works.
- Report any material encountered that is not consistent with the geotechnical profile described in the report, for a potential re-classification of the material and a review of the applicable bill rates.

5.0 CONDITIONS FOR APPROVAL

documents.title: Progress Report – Dredging Works
documents.content:
2.1 Approach Channel Dredging

Dredging of the main approach channel to the design depth of -14.5m CD was substantially completed during the first two weeks of the month. The TSHD "Eko Star" removed a total of 142,300 cubic meters of material from the outer channel section (Chainage 0+000 to 3+500). The material was disposed at the designated offshore disposal site, approximately 18 nautical miles from the port entrance.

The final survey of the approach channel was conducted on 24 January 2022 using the multibeam echo sounder. Preliminary results indicate that 98% of the surveyed area is within the allowable tolerance of ±0.3m of the design depth. A few isolated shoals remain in the area around Chainage 2+800, where the seabed is predominantly stiff clay. These shoals will be removed during the current week to bring the entire channel to the required depth.

2.2 Berth Pocket Dredging

The backhoe dredger "Apapa Pride" continued operations in the berth pockets along the container terminal quay. A total of 48,200 cubic meters was dredged from Berths 1 to 5. The dredging in the turning basin area was completed to the design depth of -13.0m CD.

Operations at Berth 7 encountered significant delays due to buried steel wire rope and old mooring chains. The debris was recovered and disposed onshore on 27 January. A total of 3.5 tonnes of scrap metal was removed from the seabed. Following debris removal, the backhoe resumed normal production of approximately 2,000 cubic meters per day.

2.3 Maintenance Dredging at Apapa Quay

A small area of siltation was observed along the quay wall at Apapa Quay, adjacent to the grain silo. This was not part of the original contract scope but was flagged by the LPA Harbour Master's office. A total of 4,350 cubic meters of soft silt was removed from this area using the CSD "River Niger" on 29 and 30 January, after the hydraulic pump repairs were completed. This work was performed on a time-charge basis and will be invoiced separately.

4.0 EQUIPMENT STATUS

4.1 TSHD "Eko Star"

The vessel operated at an average availability of 92% for the month. One day was lost on 8 January due to high swell conditions which prevented the hopper from opening its bottom doors safely at the disposal site. A minor hydraulic leak was detected in the port-side suction pipe articulation joint on 20 January; this was repaired overnight by the onboard maintenance crew and did not result in any production loss.

4.2 CSD "River Niger"

The cutter suction dredger suffered a major hydraulic pump failure on 18 January. The main pump bearing seized, causing damage to the pump casing and impeller. Replacement parts were sourced from the manufacturer's local agent in Lagos and the pump was overhauled. The dredger was back in operation on 22 January. The total downtime for this incident was 4 days.

During the downtime, the shore pipeline (600mm diameter) was inspected and two sections of worn rubber hose were replaced. The pipeline is in good condition overall.

documents.content:
4.3 Backhoe "Apapa Pride" (cont.)

The backhoe dredger operated with high availability throughout the period, recording only two days of downtime due to submerged debris encountered near the berth pockets. On 12 January, the excavator bucket struck an abandoned mooring cable embedded in the seabed, causing damage to the bucket teeth and one side plate. The cable was removed by divers from the LPA salvage team and handed over to the Harbour Master's office for disposal. Replacement bucket teeth were obtained from the local supplier, and the side plate was welded on site. The dredger resumed normal operations on 14 January.

A second interruption occurred on 25 January when the barge used for transporting the backhoe's spoil to the designated disposal ground developed a steering fault. The barge was towed back to the workshop and the hydraulic steering ram was replaced. No further issues were reported.

5.0 WEATHER AND OPERATIONAL DELAYS

Weather conditions during the month were generally favourable, with the exception of the high swell event on 8 January which affected the TSHD Eko Star. Wind speeds remained within acceptable limits for dredging operations on all other working days. Rainfall was minimal and did not cause any interruption to production.

6.0 SAFETY

One minor incident was recorded during the month. On 19 January, a deckhand on the CSD River Niger sustained a small laceration to his left forearm while handling a wire rope sling during the pump repair work. The injury was treated at the site first-aid station and did not require further medical attention. The incident was reported to the LPA Safety Office and the project HSE officer conducted a brief toolbox talk on correct sling handling and the use of gloves. No lost-time injuries were recorded.

A routine safety inspection of all dredging equipment was carried out by the LPA safety team on 27 January. The inspection covered fire extinguishers, life jackets, emergency lighting, and the condition of mooring lines. A small number of corrective actions were raised, including the replacement of expired fire extinguisher tags on the TSHD Eko Star and the repair of a cracked step on the access ladder of the backhoe Apapa Pride. These items have been scheduled for completion before the end of the first week of February.

7.0 PLANNED ACTIVITIES FOR THE COMING PERIOD

The following activities are planned for the next reporting period:

1. Continue dredging of the Outer Channel with the TSHD Eko Star, targeting the remaining shoal area near the Fairway Buoy as indicated in the latest survey.
2. Complete the final trimming of the berth pockets at Apapa Quay using the backhoe Apapa Pride, followed by a confirmation survey.
3. Mobilise the CSD River Niger to the Turning Basin to address a reported build-up of silt at the southern edge. This location was identified in the January survey as having approximately 6,800 cubic meters of material requiring removal.
4. Undertake maintenance work on the shore pipeline, including the replacement of two additional rubber hose sections that were identified as showing signs of wear during the recent inspection.
5. Carry out a calibration check on the onboard survey equipment of the TSHD Eko Star.
